name: Thomson’s dynamical heat theory
summary: Thomson rebuilt the theory of heat engines on the equivalence of heat and work, joining Joule's result with Carnot-style reasoning and Regnault's numbers.
description: Thomson explicitly combined Joule’s equivalence principle, reversible-engine reasoning attributed to Carnot and Clausius, and Regnault-based numerical results to construct a dynamical account of heat-engine performance.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: Joule's measurements made a caloric basis for Carnot's theory hard to hold, so Thomson recast engine theory on heat–work equivalence.

market.note: Commercial availability is not a milestone of a scientific knowledge result.

date.label: 1851 presentation
date.basis: Read 17 March 1851; original Transactions volume is dated 1853, and a Philosophical Magazine reprint appeared in 1852. This node dates the presentation.

events.statement: Thomson explicitly combined Joule’s equivalence principle, reversible-engine reasoning attributed to Carnot and Clausius, and Regnault-based numerical results to construct a dynamical account of heat-engine performance.
events.caveats: Thomson says his own proof preceded learning Clausius’s proof; acknowledgment is not treated as evidence that Clausius caused its invention. Historical thermal-unit conventions are not silently normalized.

links.statement: Thomson acknowledged Clausius’s proof of the reversible-engine proposition, attributed one foundational proposition jointly to Carnot and Clausius, and compared their heat-flow axioms.
links.alternatives: Thomson says his own demonstration occurred before he knew Clausius’s proof.
links.caveats: This edge records incorporation, credit and comparison in the presented theory; it does not say Clausius caused Thomson to invent his proof. The precise source event is unresolved: Thomson dates the published second-part proof to May 1850, while the 1867 Clausius collection gives March–April. The February communication is not established as the source of that proof.
links.timing: Clausius’s 1850 memoir precedes the printed 1852 account. The printed acknowledgement is not independently dated to an oral presentation.

evidence.locator: Transactions §§9 and 14, including the paragraph beginning with Clausius priority and Thomson’s independent-proof statement
evidence.supports: Explicit acknowledgment and comparison; explicit limit on a claimed invention channel.

links.statement: Thomson quotes Joule’s refined equivalent as 772.69 and uses the rounded value 772 in the numerical calculation.
links.alternatives: Thomson also discussed Rankine’s rounded value and combined the equivalent with separate experimental data.
links.caveats: Thomson describes a 32–33 °F thermal unit while Joule’s conclusion specifies water near 55–60 °F; this historical convention mismatch is retained as a limit, not silently corrected.
links.timing: 1849 communication/1850 publication precede the March 1851 presentation.

evidence.supports: Explicit quotation of Joule’s preferred 772.69 figure and use in the calculations.

links.statement: Thomson explicitly reused the Regnault-based numbers from his account two years earlier while replacing its conserved-caloric foundation with a dynamical treatment.
links.alternatives: New theoretical constraints and experimental equivalents are additional inputs.
links.caveats: Not an unqualified claim that every conclusion or approximation of 1849 survived unchanged.
links.timing: Distinct 1849 and 1851 episodes permit a genuine revision path.

evidence.supports: Names the earlier account and explains how its numerical results are reinterpreted with Joule’s equivalent.
